title: What is known about 1RB0LD_1LC0RA_1RA1LB_1LA1LE_1RF0LC_---0RE
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LD_1LC0RA_1RA1LB_1LA1LE_1RF0LC_---0RE.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Open, and probably never halting. Every so often the tape is P(n) = (10)^n A> 0. Lean (kernel) proves a computable macro step from P(n) to P(n′) or to a halt, for every n, from 21 symbolic rules. Its value follows a closed form (checked, not proved, for every n ≤ 200,000): with hk = 5·2k − k − 6 (3, 12, 31, 70, 149, …) and hk < n < hk+1, P(n) goes to P(3n − 10·2k + 3k + 14), and P(hk) halts. So the machine halts if and only if the orbit of 4 ever lands exactly on some hk. Lean checks that it does not for 200 map steps by the kernel (1086 machine steps) and 2,000 by native_decide (10798); Python follows it for 105 map steps. A target is hit by chance about once in 2k tries while k grows by about two thirds of a bit per step, so the chance of a halt later on is about 10−20,000.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 38,387 cells have been visited and 21,118 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: The macro step from P(n), for every n
claims.text: With P(n) = 0^inf (10)^n A> 0^inf, the function pstep n returns either P(n′) with an exact step count, or a halt, and pstep_sound proves for every n that the machine does exactly that. Inside: the head sweeps left turning the tape into 2n+2 ones (T phase); a doubling counter c = 1, 6, 16, 36, … eats 2c+6 ones per round through a zigzag (zig_iter, induction) and becomes 2c+4 (t_round); when fewer than 2c+6 ones are left the remainder decides: 0 or 1 left halts, otherwise a final sweep (x_iter) writes the new (10)^n′. The step counts are closed polynomials (no recursion), so pstep can be evaluated.

claims.title: The run from blank tape follows the macro step
claims.text: The machine is at P(4) after 31 steps; orbit k 4 applies the macro step k times, and orbit_sound turns any value of it into a statement about the machine.

claims.title: No halt in the first 200 macro steps (more than 10<sup>86</sup> machine steps)
claims.text: The orbit of 4 survives 200 macro steps, evaluated by the kernel (decide +kernel); the step count reached is above 1086.

claims.title: No halt in the first 2,000 macro steps (more than 10<sup>798</sup> machine steps)
claims.text: The same for 2,000 macro steps with native_decide; n then has 1,326 bits.

claims.title: The closed form of the macro step
claims.text: For hk < n < hk+1 with r = n − hk − 1: n′ = 5·2k − 1 + 3r in 12r² + (40·2k+6)r + (100·4k+23)/3 − 10·2k steps; P(hk) halts. A Python transcription of the Lean pstep agrees with this for every 1 ≤ n ≤ 200,000 (the closed form itself is not proved in Lean). Direct simulation agrees too: all 16 P-events of the run from blank tape up to 1010 steps (n = 4, 9, 24, 52, 99, 163, 198, 303, 618, 1246, 2493, 4957, 9792, 19180, 37107, 70411; the last at step 9,108,900,940) match in n and step.

claims.title: 10<sup>5</sup> macro steps without a halt
claims.text: Python iterates the closed form (exact big integers) for 10<sup>5</sup> macro steps from P(4) without landing on an h<sub>k</sub>; n then has 66,605 bits and the step count is about 10<sup>40,100</sup>.

claims.title: Probviously non-halting
claims.text: At level k, n′ ranges over about 5·2<sup>k</sup> values in steps of 3, and on average 2/3 of a target h<sub>j</sub> per level lies among them; treating r as random, the chance of a halt is about 2<sup>−k</sup> per macro step. The level grows by about 0.66 per macro step (n multiplies by about 1.58), so the sum converges: from the end of the 10<sup>5</sup> checked steps (k about 66,605) the chance that it ever halts is about 10<sup>−20,000</sup>. The machine is a cousin of the “Cryptids”: its halting is a question about the digits of an orbit, which no known method decides.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. It halts if and only if the orbit of 4 under the map reaches some hk (given the closed form; with only the Lean macro step: if and only if pstep ever returns a halt along the orbit).

explainer.lede: Probably never, but nobody can prove it. This machine keeps rewriting its tape as (10)^n and then computes a new n from the old one with a rule that looks like a Collatz map with a binary counter inside. It stops only if n ever lands exactly on one of the numbers 3, 12, 31, 70, 149, 308, … In 2,000 rounds (more than 10798 steps, checked in Lean) it never has.

facts.text: Every round P(n) → P(n′) or halt is proved in Lean for every n, with exact step counts.
No halt in 2,000 rounds (Lean, native_decide); 200 rounds and 10<sup>86</sup> steps by the kernel alone.
Chance of a halt after the 10<sup>5</sup> rounds followed in Python, if n behaves randomly.

sections.heading: A Collatz-like map with a binary counter inside
html: Every so often the tape is just n copies of 10 with the head in state A to the right of them. Call this P(n). From blank tape the machine reaches P(4) after 31 steps, then P(9), P(24), P(52), P(99), P(163), … Between two such moments it does three things:

It sweeps left and turns the whole tape into 2n+2 ones. Then a small counter at the left end, starting at c = 1, repeatedly eats 2c+6 of the ones and doubles itself plus 4: c runs 1, 6, 16, 36, 76, … = 5·2j − 4. The number k of complete rounds is the level of n, about log2 n. When fewer than 2c+6 ones are left, a final sweep writes the next block of 10s. The result is a single rule:

level khalts at n =other nnext n
134 – 113n − 3
21213 – 303n − 20
33132 – 693n − 57
47071 – 1483n − 134
5149150 – 3073n − 291

In general, with hk = 5·2k − k − 6, every n strictly between hk and hk+1 goes to 3n − 10·2k + 3k + 14. So n is multiplied by 3 and then pulled back by the counter, which ends up multiplying it by about 1.58 per round on average. The rounds take about n² steps each.

sections.heading: Only by landing exactly on 3, 12, 31, 70, 149, …
html: The machine halts when the last round of the counter uses up the ones exactly (0 or 1 left over). That happens precisely when n is one of the numbers hk = 3, 12, 31, 70, 149, 308, 627, 1266, …, just below the powers of two times 5.

The run from blank tape goes 4, 9, 24, 52, 99, 163, 198, 303, 618, 1246, 2493, 4957, 9792, … and has to dodge a target at every level. The next n is 3r plus a fixed number, for r spread over about 5·2k values, and only a few hj are in reach, so a random-looking n hits one with chance about 2−k. Since k grows by about two thirds per round, these chances add up to something tiny: having dodged the targets for the first 105 rounds (followed exactly in Python), the chance that it ever halts is about 10−20,000.

Proving that it never halts would mean proving that this orbit avoids a sparse set forever: a question about the digits of 3-and-2 arithmetic of the same kind as the Collatz problem. That is why bbchallenge lists the machine as a potential Cryptid.

sections.heading: Proved in Lean: every round, and 10<sup>798</sup> steps
html:
• Kernel: 21 symbolic rules (generated by py/rules.py), the counter loop and the final sweep by induction, and from them a function pstep giving the round from P(n) for every n, with its exact step count or a halt.
  • Kernel: blank tape reaches P(4) in 31 steps; 200 rounds without a halt, more than 1086 steps.
  • native_decide: 2,000 rounds without a halt, more than 10798 steps.
  • Checked by program, not proved: the closed form above (for every n ≤ 200,000), 16 rounds against the real machine up to 1010 steps, and 105 rounds of the map.
  • Open: whether the orbit ever hits an hk.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.524). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.055).
After 109 steps the tape spans 38,387 cells (34,708 left of the start, 41 right), with a density of 1s of 0.55.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

family: Collatz-like n → 3n − 10·2<sup>k</sup> + 3k + 14 with a doubling counter (level k)
summary: Provably the orbit of a Collatz-like map on P(n) = (10)<sup>n</sup> A>: at level k (h<sub>k</sub> < n < h<sub>k+1</sub>, h<sub>k</sub> = 5·2<sup>k</sup> − k − 6) n → 3n − 10·2<sup>k</sup> + 3k + 14, and it halts exactly when n = h<sub>k</sub>; Lean checks no halt for 2,000 map steps (10<sup>798</sup> machine steps).
